items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 4, 2026
items.excerpt: 04 November 2026• Update: 04 November 2026 Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Wednesday, including US Democrats projected to win both houses of Congress in midterm elections, US midterms delivering wave of historic firsts across states, and President Donald Trump’s pledging to end US financial aid to Israel by year’s end. Democrats were projected to take control of both chambers of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, delivering a major political setback to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, according to US media projections. The party made significant gains beyond its traditional strongholds, winning key races in states that overwhelmingly supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election, including Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, and Kansas. The scale of the Democratic wave was still becoming clear early Wednesday, but the results pointed to widespread voter dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, particularly over the economy, rising living costs, and the president's decision to launch a war against Iran in February. - US midterms deliver wave of historic firsts across states, Congress Tuesday’s US midterm elections produced a series of historic firsts in races for governor, Senate and the House of Representatives. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state, as well as Georgia’s first woman and first Black governor. Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland won in New Mexico to become the first Native American woman elected governor in US history, while Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the US Senate. In New Jersey, Democrat Adam Hamawy won the 12th Congressional District to become the state’s first Muslim member of Congress. Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa became the state’s first Latina governor, while Republican Byron Donalds was elected Florida’s first Black governor. In Ohio, Amy Acton became the state’s first woman and first Jewish governor, while David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor. Illinois Democrat Juliana Stratton’s Senate victory also means three Black women will serve simultaneously in the chamber for the first time. - Trump pledges end to US aid for Israel by year’s end US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Washington will stop providing financial aid to Israel by year's end under an agreement reached with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping, and they're fine with it because, you know, they've become a very successful country that are not in need, and we won't be paying any more to Israel," Trump told Fox News. He added that Washington would still provide assistance if needed, describing Israel as a regional partner with whom the US has maintained "a tremendous relationship," with Tel Aviv being the smaller partner.

items.title: Strong US GDP Growth Comes With Higher Inflation
items.excerpt: The US economy posted stronger-than-expected growth in the third quarter, but accelerating inflation added to the economic challenges facing President Donald Trump as the midterm elections take place. ... Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annualized rate of 3.4% between July and September, beating market expectations, the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said. The growth rate was higher than the 2.2% recorded in the second quarter. The BEA attributed the expansion to increases in investment, consumer spending and government spending, partly offset by a decline in exports. The figures presented a mixed picture for policymakers and voters, as stronger economic activity coincided with persistent price pressures. The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.6% year over year in September, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, the PCE price index increased 0.5% in September, according to the BEA's report on personal income and outlays. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 3.1% from a year earlier, compared with 3.0% in August. The acceleration in inflation could complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring price increases back toward its 2% target, particularly as the economy continues to expand. items.title: The Fed can't fix this inflation. It's a mechanical weight, not a demand problem
items.excerpt: 11/02/2026 16:28:22 GMT # The Fed can't fix this inflation. ... Joshua Gibson FXStreet Producer prices are rising 2.6 points faster than consumer prices, the widest gap since 2022, because most of the Iran war's costs haven't reached shoppers yet. The part that has is fuel, and rate hikes can't make fuel cheaper. The Producer Price Index (PPI), which tracks what US businesses get for the goods and services they sell, rose 6.3% through September. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7%. In February, the last full month before the Iran war, the gap between them was about a point. It's now 2.6 points, the widest since April 2022. Most of the war's costs still fall on businesses, and shoppers pay at the pump. The Federal Reserve (Fed) raised its rate to 3.75-4.00% in September and held it in October, with two members voting for another hike. The number that matters most for inflation is the price of Brent, the main global Oil price, and no one at the Fed sets it. ## Seven months of war, a tenth of a point outside energy Energy prices, which cover gasoline and the power and fuel used in homes, rose 20.4% through September, and gasoline alone rose 34.2%. Energy makes up about 7% of the CPI, so it added about 1.3 percentage points to the 3.7% total. In February it added almost nothing. Everything else barely changed. Prices outside food and energy, often called underlying inflation, were up 2.6%, a tenth of a point faster than in February. Food prices are rising more slowly than they were before the war. So almost all of the 1.3-point rise in inflation since February is the fuel bill, and with Brent trading near its highest since mid-2022, that bill hasn't gone away. ... Fuel came through in full. Energy prices are up about a third for businesses since February and about a fifth for shoppers. Diesel at the pump costs about two-thirds more, and airfares are up 22.4% on the year. Freight and packaging have reached businesses but not shoppers yet. Long-distance trucking rates are up a fifth since February and cardboard boxes 9%. A grocery chain in the Richmond Fed's district reported in October that trucking a head of lettuce now costs more than the lettuce.

items.title: Interrogating Reality: The Fed’s Wait-and-See Approach | BauerFinancial
items.excerpt: ## JRN by Bauer 43:43, November 4, 2026 ... Overall inflation was up 3.7% in September, but when volatile food and energy prices are removed from the equation, CORE inflation was actually up much less (2.6%). Inflation has been stubbornly resting above its 2% target for 5½ years (since April 2021) and peaked in 2022. Exactly what month it peaked depends on which measure of inflation you use (see chart below). The Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index (PCE) are two common measures of inflation – both measuring how prices change over time. The PCE contains a larger “basket of goods” in its index than the CPI. The PCE also includes spending made by, as well as on behalf of, consumers whereas the CPI only includes out-of-pocket expenditures by urban households. For these reasons, the PCE is both more encompassing and less volatile than the CPI.

items.title: Democrats seize Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump. Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Trump’s stewardship of the country. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago. In South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate. And in Texas, the biggest Republican state, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning a Senate seat and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott. The results will usher in a new era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in Trump. Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise. "There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America," said Chuck Schumer, the party’s Senate minority leader. "Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must deliver." Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, has exercised an iron grip on his party for most of the last decade. But the new balance of power in Washington may accelerate his lame-duck status, as attention turns toward the 2028 presidential race and potential successors begin competing for political influence in a post-Trump world. Despite worries from Democrats that Trump might seek to overturn the election results, as he did in 2020, the president accepted the outcome, congratulating Democrats in an interview with Fox News. He also said he would work with Democrats on issues such as immigration, though he threatened to veto any "insane" bills they passed. ... Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump’s tariff policy and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House. ... Democrats ran the table in the House races thought to be especially competitive, winning all 20 of the contests decided so far. Meanwhile, an unprecedented Republican gambit to redraw several House districts to make ... According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed. In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

items.title: Democrats flip four governorships, extending the party’s inroads into red states
items.excerpt: Nov. 4, 2026, 12:37 AM EST / Updated Nov. 4, 2026, 2:23 AM EST By Adam Edelman Democrats clinched a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years in Tuesday’s elections, further punctuating the party’s success across the map. Seizing on a broadly toxic political climate for Republicans, Democrats flipped control of four governor’s mansions in states President Donald Trump carried in 2024, while maintaining power in several other battleground states. Democratic candidates wrested control of governor’s mansions in Georgia, Iowa, Texas and Ohio. The most shocking flip came in Texas — a state Trump won two years ago by nearly 14 points, where the last Democratic governor was elected more than three decades ago. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, overcoming a massive spending deficit to become the state’s first Latina chief executive. ... Democrats also made history in Georgia, where former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, flipping control of the battleground state office for the first time in 24 years. Bottoms’ victory means she will become the first Black female governor in U.S. history. Bottoms is one of three Black gubernatorial candidates who won Tuesday, along with Democratic Gov. Wes Moore in Maryland and Republican Byron Donalds in Florida. There has never been more than one Black governor serving at a time before. In Iowa, State Auditor Rob Sand beat Republican Zach Lahn, making him the first Democrat to be elected to lead the state in two decades. Trump won Iowa in 2024 by 13 points. And in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton beat Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, succeeding Republican Mike DeWine. Republicans had entered Tuesday’s elections with a 26-24 majority in governor’s races. ... Thirty-six gubernatorial contests were on the ballot this year. ... Democrats also held on to gubernatorial power in critical swing states. In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley defeated GOP Rep. Tom Tiffany to succeed two-term Democrat Tony Evers. Meanwhile, Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs won re-election over Republican Andy Biggs, casting herself as a moderate in a state Trump won by 5 percentage points in 2024. In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won re-election by more than 20 points, while in Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson defeated Republican John James to succeed Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Democratic candidates remain locked in tight races in Nevada and Kansas early Wednesday. In Kansas, state Sen. Cindy Holscher was locked in a tight contest with Republican Ty Masterson. Despite Kansas’ history as a solidly Republican state, it has had a Democratic governor for the last eight years.

During the session, a fan asked her what advice she would give young girls about making career choices. Responding to the question on Tuesday, Shraddha revealed that she turned down several film offers, including lucrative projects, after Stree 2 because she wanted to wait for the right story. She said, "I would share about myself. After Stree 2, I was offered a lot of films and money as well, but I had decided that until I get that perfect story, I won't sign anything. items.excerpt: - AP - Nov 4, 2026 - 2 hrs ago Movie Review: In ‘Wild Horse Nine,’ death looms for a CIA goon John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play a couple of bickering CIA agents on a trip to Easter Island in Martin McDonagh's “Wild Horse Nine.” The dark comedy is set in 1973, just before the military coup in Chile, and Malkovich's character is getting a little loose lipped about the plans. In her review for The Associated Press, film writer Lindsey Bahr writes that while the territory and themes may be familiar for McDonagh, the actors elevate even the less savory clunkers. “Wild Horse Nine” is rated R and is playing in theaters starting Friday. LONDON (AP) — Jurors have started deliberating in Russell Brand's trial on charges of rape and sexual assault. After three weeks of evidence, the judge at London’s Southwark Crown Court instructed the jury to reach a unanimous decision. Brand, who is free on bail, has attended court daily with his wife. Six women accuse him of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutors claim Brand was a "sexual predator" during that time. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty, stating his encounters were consensual. His lawyer argued the claims were influenced by a 2023 documentary. Brand rose to fame in the early 2000s and now has a large online following. The new animated “The Cat in the Hat” has plenty of tricks up its sleeve, says Associated Press critic Mark Kennedy. Directed by Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni, the film takes a Marvel-style approach, with world-saving stakes and a mysterious villain. Bill Hader voices the Cat, who works for a corporate conglomerate tasked with cheering up kids. The film features stylized animation and a star-studded voice cast, including Giancarlo Esposito and Bowen Yang. Despite its whimsical source material, the movie's messaging feels muddled, and the plot is overloaded with Things. It hits theaters Friday and is rated PG. ... NEW YORK (AP) — Tony Butala, co-founder of the Grammy-nominated trio The Lettermen, has died at age 87. The band's media coordinator confirmed his death and shared a statement from the band expressing deep sadness and sending condolences to his family and friends. Butala died Sunday. Butala's career began in childhood, singing professionally by age 7. In the late ‘50s, he co-founded The Lettermen with Jim Pike and Bob Engemann. They became one of the most popular vocal groups of the 1960s, with hits like “The Way You Look Tonight” and “When I Fall in Love.” Butala was the last surviving member of the trio’s original lineup. In 2020, Butala and The Lettermen received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Even Godzilla can be felled by an old hazard: the sophomore slump. Though Godzilla has been stomping around for more than half a century, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is a sequel. It follows the quite excellent, Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One,” a reset for the kaiju franchise that brought Godzilla back to its postwar Japan roots. Like its predecessor, the follow-up marries human-scaled drama with a flair for stompy-stomp spectacle. Yet AP Film Writer Jake Coyle says those calibrations are slightly off in “Godzilla Minus Zero.” In his review, Coyle writes that the melodrama on the ground overtakes the movie, sagging it with a bloated story that leaves you pining for the big guy to turn up again. NEW YORK (AP) — David Mendizábal is directing a revival of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s "In the Heights," a musical that was Mendizábal's introduction to theater. The show, running for three weeks at New York City Center, features a new cast of Latino artists. Mendizábal emphasizes the importance of showcasing Latino communities, especially now. Miranda, who starred in the original production, reflects on the musical's enduring relevance. The revival comes amid immigration tensions, highlighting themes of gentrification and community. New and old cast members say the musical remains a celebration of the Latino immigrant experience, with its messages resonating strongly today. NEW YORK (AP) — My Chemical Romance has hit No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with “The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Deluxe Edition).” This reissue of their 2006 rock opera includes six bonus tracks. Back then, it debuted at No. 2 due to competition from Disney’s “Hannah Montana” soundtrack. The reissue's success is driven by 20 physical variants and a significant increase in album sales. The band’s reunion and anniversary tour have also fueled interest. Nostalgic fans and new listeners are connecting with the album's unique style and themes. This marks the longest wait for an album to reach No. 1. WASHINGTON (AP) — The Kennedy Center has announced that Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell will be honored at this year's Kennedy Center Honors. The event will take place away from the iconic venue for the first time due to President Donald Trump's legal battle over renovations and naming rights. The nominees have had substantial careers in their fields. Mamet is a renowned playwright, while Mandrell is a Country Music Hall of Fame member. Anka, a longtime friend of Trump, has rewritten “My Way” with MAGA-themed lyrics. The ceremony will be held on December 7 at Washington's Capital One Arena.
